headline: JUI-F to protest anti-encroachment drive, ‘propaganda’ against Fazl on 15th
description: Asks govt to focus on its ‘mandate of eliminating terrorism’
author: Bureau Report
article_text:
PESHAWAR: The Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Tuesday directed its district chapters to hold street protests on Nov 15 against the ongoing drive against encroachments and “propaganda” against the party and its leadership.

Addressing a presser at the party’s provincial headquarters here after a meeting of the JUI-F KP executive council, the party’s provincial emir, Senator Maulana Attaur Rahman, said the meeting discussed “baseless and fake propaganda” against the party and its leaders, actions being taken in the name of removing encroachments and party chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman’s stand on mineral reserves.

He said it appeared that the emergency had been imposed in the province not to eliminate terrorism but to remove encroachments.

Asks govt to focus on its ‘mandate of eliminating terrorism’

Mr Atta asked the current provincial government to focus on its mandate of eliminating terrorism instead of targeting public properties across the province in the name of removing encroachments.

He said that if encroachment removal was the government’s only objective, there had been no need to impose governor’s rule and emergency in the province.

The JUI-F KP emir said the crackdown on encroachments amounted to an operation against the province’s peaceful people, who were earning livelihoods through businesses.

He said the party’s executive council had also expressed concern over the actions taken in the name of removing encroachments across the province, especially in Peshawar, including the demolition of legal shops, plazas, houses and mosques.

The council also expressed complete solidarity with the trader community and affected shopkeepers.

Mr Atta said the forum insisted that constructions on government land fell under the category of encroachments.

He said people had the right to know the justification for demolishing plazas and houses without serving notices despite the owners having obtained no-objection certificates and approval of building plans from government institutions.

The emir said that the government should assure people that compensation would be paid for properties it acquired under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act.

He also said the party had expressed concern over “irresponsible” statements by the KP governor and the adviser on information regarding the party’s Mufti Mahmood Markaz.

Mr Atta said that the complex, spread over four kanals, had been constructed after the building plans were approved by the Peshawar Development Authority.

He added that the administration had closed the service road in front of the building due to security reasons.

The JUI-F leader said the executive council fully endorsed Maulana Fazl’s stand on mineral resources.

He added that the province’s mineral resources were being transported through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor route after the closure of roads.

“The nation should be informed about the agreements made with any country and that the party’s KP chapter stands fully with the party chief on this stance,” he said.

Mr Atta said that the council had also decided to launch an awareness campaign on the issue. He said protest demonstrations would be held in all districts of the province on Sunday (Nov 15).

He said the party’s general council had condemned “one-sided propaganda, fake statements and immoral videos” released against the JUI-F chief and other leaders. “Instead of providing reasoned and factual answers to Maulana Fazl’s questions, the federal government had resorted to cheap tactics.

The government’s paid TikTokers can’t divert the JUI-F from its mission through unethical acts and cheap tactics,” he said.

Regarding the merged tribal districts, Mr Atta said the government was trying to reverse the Fata-KP merger.

He, however, said the party believed that both the merger and any decision to reverse it should be made in accordance with the wishes of the people instead of being imposed on them.

Mr Atta said the meeting also expressed concern over the arrest of JUI-F workers in different parts of the country and notices issued by various institutions.

headline: Oil rises from two-month low as Hormuz shipping attacks offset Iran truce hopes
description: Oil prices rise after falling to two-month lows in the previous session, as the market swung between hopes for a...
article_text:
Oil prices rise after falling to two-month lows in the previous session, as the market swung between hopes for a de-escalation in the Iran war and concerns about ongoing attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reports.

Brent futures have climbed 71 cents, or 0.78 per cent, to $92.20 a barrel by 0119 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude have risen 49 cents, or 0.57pc, to $86.53.

New data shows that 37 ships were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways in October, the highest monthly total since the start of the war, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. And 10 attacks have been recorded so far in November.

headline: Russian and Iranian diplomats discuss Middle East conflicts in Moscow
description: Russia and Iran have held consultations in Moscow on regional issues, with a focus on resolving conflicts in the...
article_text:
Russia and Iran have held consultations in Moscow on regional issues, with a focus on resolving conflicts in the Middle East and North Africa, the Russian Foreign Ministry says, Al Jazeera cites Iran’s state news agency IRNA.

Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Borisenko has met Mehdi Shoushtari, the director general for West Asia and North Africa at Iran’s Foreign Ministry, who travelled to Moscow to take part in consultations between the two foreign ministries on regional issues.

Borisenko has also met the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation’s deputy secretary-general for political affairs, Yousef Aldobeay, who was in Moscow for an international forum on collective security, according to IRNA.

They have discussed rising tensions in the Gulf and the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, and stressed the need to resolve crises through political and diplomatic means, in line with international law, it adds.

headline: Public Accounts Committee seeks to delay power firms’ sell-off until asset valuation
description: Concerns raised that government is relying on outdated valuations of public assets.
author: Jamal Shahid
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: The Pub­lic Accounts Committee (PAC) on Tuesday propo­sed deferring the privatisation of power companies, expected to take place in January, until their assets, machinery, land and other properties are properly assessed and revalued to prevent potential losses to the national exchequer.

The proposal came after Auditor General of Paki­stan Maqbool Ahmad Gon­dal raised concerns that the government was relying on outdated valuations of public assets during a meeting of the PAC to examine the audit reports of the Power Division and its attached entities for 2024-25.

The committee observed that the management had failed to revalue fixed ass­ets worth Rs624.47 billion.

The Auditor General’s office also pointed out that the companies had not tag­ged their assets, reflecting negligence in complying with directives of the Nati­o­nal Electric Power Regul­a­tory Authority (Nepra).

It said property, plant and equipment were key components of financial statements, and inaccurate valuations could distort a company’s overall financial position.

PAC Chairperson Shah­ida Begum said the actual value of the assets needed to be determined and properly categorised before proceeding with privatisation.

“Until we know their exact value, how can we privatise them? If the assets are sold without proper valuation, it will definitely result in a loss for the government,” she said.

She called for another meeting in three weeks to review the privatisation process and ensure that the assets were assigned their correct market values before further steps were taken.

The Privatisation Commission and the Power Division were directed to submit detailed reports at the next meeting.

Rs8.6bn payments questioned

The committee also examined audit objections concerning payments of Rs8.648bn borne by electricity consumers because of poor planning, faulty procurement of equipment and deficiencies in the performance of a grid station and its associated transmission line.

During a performance audit of the power transmission system for wind projects in the Sindh Wind Corridor, auditors found that Rs8.6bn had been paid to wind power producers under the Non-Pro­ject Missed Volume (NPMV) mechanism.

The projects were ready to supply electricity, but the 220kV Jhim­pir Grid Station could not handle their full output because of frequ­ent tripping and system instability.

The management attributed the losses to faulty equipment procurement and worsening climate change conditions.

MNA Munazza Hassan took exception to the response when National Grid Managing Director Altaf Hussain attributed the loss to climate change. Calling it criminal negligence, MNA Shazia Marri lamented resistance to renewable technologies.

Regarding the Rs8.6bn amount, she said the matter had not been settled and that further details would be sought at the next meeting, along with the relevant inquiry report.

She said the issue would be taken up again after the required information and assessments had been completed.

Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

headline: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Hegseth
description: Motion to send articles to Republican-led Judiciary Committee passes 211-204; had eight of 11 Democrats who did not vote opposed it, motion would have failed.
author: Reuters
article_text:
Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, winning a reprieve for the polarising Pentagon chief before Democrats take control of Congress next year and possibly try again.

The vote on a procedural motion came just hours after Hegseth blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce and delivered a defiant defence of his record at the helm of the US military, winning praise from US President Donald Trump.

The chamber voted 211 to 204 in favour of a motion to refer eight articles of impeachment to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, a move that the sponsor of the impeachment push, US Representative Thomas Massie, warned would kill it.

Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, had hoped to draw votes from Republicans upset with Hegseth’s policies and wary of the unpopularity of the war on Iran, but no other Republicans joined him.

Democrats had voiced strong support for the impeachment effort. But 11 Democrats, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, did not vote.

If eight of them had, the procedural measure would have been defeated, paving the way for a full House impeachment vote. Pelosi’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on why she missed the vote.

Trump cheered the results in a social media post, saying the effort to impeach Hegseth “has miserably FAILED!”

In a sign that the impeachment episode may have drawn Trump and Hegseth closer together, Trump added that Hegseth’s performance on Iran, Venezuela and other issues “led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”

Hegseth would have been the first US defence secretary to be impeached. The last time any civilian leader of the US military was impeached was in 1876, when William Belknap held the title “secretary of war”.

Hegseth calls himself secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and “woke” when he took office last year. Trump cannot change the name of the Defence Department without approval from Congress.

Iran war anger

Voter anger over the war on Iran, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress, which takes office in January, to act to end the war once and for all.

Although Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned the war and blamed it for the Republicans’ midterm rout, he voiced support for Hegseth on Tuesday.

“This isn’t about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon,” Vance wrote on social media.

Before the vote, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday: “Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America’s national security, and he’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran.”

Hegseth has repeatedly defended the conflict, calling Trump courageous and saying Iran’s military has been left in ruins. He also said his orders to US forces were lawful, despite Massie’s accusations of “high crimes and misdemeanours” ranging from the war itself to the US military raid in January to depose Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

“History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now,” Hegseth said on Tuesday at his first Pentagon briefing in six months.

Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next Congress. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.

A Democratic-led push to impeach Hegseth could be far more intense, with lawmakers calling in top brass to testify, including generals and admirals fired by Hegseth who have remained silent so far. Hegseth, who has railed against diversity efforts at the Pentagon, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who is Black, and the Navy’s top admiral, a woman, among others.

In such an effort, Democrats could also raise other issues concerning to voters including Pentagon policy toward Ukraine and the US military’s strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Caribbean and Pacific waters.

Some Republicans say Hegseth’s strained relations with Congress are becoming a political liability as the Trump administration seeks a huge increase in the military’s budget to $1.5 trillion from $950 billion.

Massie said he was disappointed by the vote, comparing Republicans to passengers content to go down with the Titanic.

“They know it’s a sinking ship but committed to stay on board,” he said.

Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, had hoped to draw votes from Republicans upset with Hegseth’s policies and wary of the unpopularity of the war on Iran, but no other Republicans joined him.

Democrats had voiced strong support for the impeachment effort. But 11 Democrats, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, did not vote.

If eight of them had, the procedural measure would have been defeated, paving the way for a full House impeachment vote. Pelosi’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on why she missed the vote.

Trump cheered the results in a social media post, saying the effort to impeach Hegseth “has miserably FAILED!”

In a sign that the impeachment episode may have drawn Trump and Hegseth closer together, Trump added that Hegseth’s performance on Iran, Venezuela and other issues “led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”

Hegseth would have been the first US defence secretary to be impeached. The last time any civilian leader of the US military was impeached was in 1876, when William Belknap held the title “secretary of war”.

Hegseth calls himself secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and “woke” when he took office last year. Trump cannot change the name of the Defence Department without approval from Congress.

Iran war anger

Voter anger over the war on Iran, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress, which takes office in January, to act to end the war once and for all.

Although Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned the war and blamed it for the Republicans’ midterm rout, he voiced support for Hegseth on Tuesday.

“This isn’t about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon,” Vance wrote on social media.

Before the vote, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday: “Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America’s national security, and he’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran.”

Hegseth has repeatedly defended the conflict, calling Trump courageous and saying Iran’s military has been left in ruins. He also said his orders to US forces were lawful, despite Massie’s accusations of “high crimes and misdemeanours” ranging from the war itself to the US military raid in January to depose Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

“History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now,” Hegseth said on Tuesday at his first Pentagon briefing in six months.

Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next Congress. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.

A Democratic-led push to impeach Hegseth could be far more intense, with lawmakers calling in top brass to testify, including generals and admirals fired by Hegseth who have remained silent so far. Hegseth, who has railed against diversity efforts at the Pentagon, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who is Black, and the Navy’s top admiral, a woman, among others.

In such an effort, Democrats could also raise other issues concerning to voters including Pentagon policy toward Ukraine and the US military’s strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Caribbean and Pacific waters.

Some Republicans say Hegseth’s strained relations with Congress are becoming a political liability as the Trump administration seeks a huge increase in the military’s budget to $1.5 trillion from $950 billion.

Massie said he was disappointed by the vote, comparing Republicans to passengers content to go down with the Titanic.

“They know it’s a sinking ship but committed to stay on board,” he said.

headline: Rain, snow in northern parts of the country from today
description: A shallow westerly wave is approaching the western and northern par­ts of the country; system likely to intensify on Nov 12, may persist until the morning of Nov 14.
author: Aamir Yasin
article_text:
RAWALPINDI: The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) has forecast rain, wind and thunderstorms, with snowfall over the hills, in the upper parts of the country over the next two to three days, urging the authorities concerned to take precautionary measures to prevent any untoward incident, particularly in hilly areas.

According to the Met Off­ice, a shallow westerly wave is approaching the western and northern par­ts of the country. The system is likely to intensify on Nov 12 and may persist over the upper regions until the morning of Nov 14.

In Khyber Pakhtu­nk­hwa, under the influence of this weather system, rain, wind and thundersto­rms, accompanied by isolated heavy falls and hailstorms, are expected in Dir, Chitral, Swat, Koh­is­t­an, Shangla, Battagram, Mansehra, Abbottabad, Haripur, Buner, Malak­and, Bajaur, Mohmand,

Kohat, Peshawar, Charsa­dda, Nowshera, Mar­dan, Swabi, Khyber, Orakzai, Kurram, Hangu, Lakki Mar­wat, Karak, Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan and Waziristan from the evening/night of Nov 10 until the morning of Nov 14, with occasional breaks. Snowfall is also likely over the mountains during this period.

In Punjab and Islamabad, light rain, wind and thunderstorms are expected in the capital city, the Potohar region, Mianwali, Khushab, Bhakkar, Sargodha, Murree and adjoining areas on Wednesday (today). More rain, wind and thunderstorms are forecast for Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Murree, Galiyat, Attock, Chakwal, Jhelum, Mandi Bahauddin, Gujrat, Gujranwala, Hafizabad, Wazirabad, Lahore, Kasur, Sheikhupura, Sialkot, Narowal, Mianwali, Khushab and Sargodha on Nov 12 and 13, with occasional breaks.

Rain, wind and thunderstorms are also expected in Dera Ghazi Khan, Layyah, Bhakkar and Multan on Nov 12. Isolated hailstorms are also likely during the period.

Snowfall over hills

Meanwhile, rain, wind and thunderstorms, accompanied by snowfall over the hills, are expected in Azad Kashmir, including Neelum Valley, Muzaffarabad, Rawalakot, Poonch, Hattian, Bagh, Haveli, Sudhanoti, Kotli, Bhimber and Mirpur, and Gilgit-Baltistan, including Diamir, Astore, Ghizer, Skardu, Hunza, Gilgit, Ghanche and Shigar, until the afternoon of Nov 14, with occasional breaks.

Dry weather

Mainly dry weather is expected to prevail across most districts of Sindh and Balochistan. However, isolated rain, wind and thunderstorms, accompanied by hailstorms, are expected in Duki, Harnai, Pishin, Sherani, Surab, Zhob, Barkhan, Musakhel, Quetta, Ziarat, Chaman, Qila Abdullah, Qila Saifullah, Kalat and Khuzdar on the night of Nov 11 and Nov 12.

Impacts and advisories

The Met Office advised farmers to plan their agricultural activities in accordance with the prevailing and forecast weather conditions.

It warned that light snowfall over high mountains and glaciers could occur during the wet spell. Foggy conditions are also likely to develop in patches over the plains following the spell.

Daytime temperatures are expected to fall by 2-4 degrees Celsius during the forecast period.

The department urged provincial and district authorities to remain vigilant and take all necessary precautionary measures to avoid any untoward incidents during the forecast period.

Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

RAWALPINDI: The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) has forecast rain, wind and thunderstorms, with snowfall over the hills, in the upper parts of the country over the next two to three days, urging the authorities concerned to take precautionary measures to prevent any untoward incident, particularly in hilly areas.

According to the Met Off­ice, a shallow westerly wave is approaching the western and northern par­ts of the country. The system is likely to intensify on Nov 12 and may persist over the upper regions until the morning of Nov 14.

In Khyber Pakhtu­nk­hwa, under the influence of this weather system, rain, wind and thundersto­rms, accompanied by isolated heavy falls and hailstorms, are expected in Dir, Chitral, Swat, Koh­is­t­an, Shangla, Battagram, Mansehra, Abbottabad, Haripur, Buner, Malak­and, Bajaur, Mohmand,

Kohat, Peshawar, Charsa­dda, Nowshera, Mar­dan, Swabi, Khyber, Orakzai, Kurram, Hangu, Lakki Mar­wat, Karak, Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan and Waziristan from the evening/night of Nov 10 until the morning of Nov 14, with occasional breaks. Snowfall is also likely over the mountains during this period.

In Punjab and Islamabad, light rain, wind and thunderstorms are expected in the capital city, the Potohar region, Mianwali, Khushab, Bhakkar, Sargodha, Murree and adjoining areas on Wednesday (today). More rain, wind and thunderstorms are forecast for Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Murree, Galiyat, Attock, Chakwal, Jhelum, Mandi Bahauddin, Gujrat, Gujranwala, Hafizabad, Wazirabad, Lahore, Kasur, Sheikhupura, Sialkot, Narowal, Mianwali, Khushab and Sargodha on Nov 12 and 13, with occasional breaks.

Rain, wind and thunderstorms are also expected in Dera Ghazi Khan, Layyah, Bhakkar and Multan on Nov 12. Isolated hailstorms are also likely during the period.

Snowfall over hills

Meanwhile, rain, wind and thunderstorms, accompanied by snowfall over the hills, are expected in Azad Kashmir, including Neelum Valley, Muzaffarabad, Rawalakot, Poonch, Hattian, Bagh, Haveli, Sudhanoti, Kotli, Bhimber and Mirpur, and Gilgit-Baltistan, including Diamir, Astore, Ghizer, Skardu, Hunza, Gilgit, Ghanche and Shigar, until the afternoon of Nov 14, with occasional breaks.

Dry weather

Mainly dry weather is expected to prevail across most districts of Sindh and Balochistan. However, isolated rain, wind and thunderstorms, accompanied by hailstorms, are expected in Duki, Harnai, Pishin, Sherani, Surab, Zhob, Barkhan, Musakhel, Quetta, Ziarat, Chaman, Qila Abdullah, Qila Saifullah, Kalat and Khuzdar on the night of Nov 11 and Nov 12.

Impacts and advisories

The Met Office advised farmers to plan their agricultural activities in accordance with the prevailing and forecast weather conditions.

It warned that light snowfall over high mountains and glaciers could occur during the wet spell. Foggy conditions are also likely to develop in patches over the plains following the spell.

Daytime temperatures are expected to fall by 2-4 degrees Celsius during the forecast period.

The department urged provincial and district authorities to remain vigilant and take all necessary precautionary measures to avoid any untoward incidents during the forecast period.

Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

headline: Development spending stalls despite surplus
description: Ministries, divisions utilise just Rs103.87bn in July-October against Rs1tr allocation.
author: Khaleeq Kiani
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: The country’s Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP) spending in the first four months of the current fiscal year struggled at only 10 per cent of the annual allocation.

Total PSDP spending in the first four months (July-October) of 2026-27 amounted to Rs103.87bn — 10.4pc of the Rs1trillion allocation, according to the Ministry of Planning and Development. Actual utilisation was far lower than the Rs412.3bn authorised by the Planning Commission.

This alarming spending pattern on public-interest projects, which is affecting living standards and economic growth, has emerged despite a healthy 0.8pc budget surplus posted in the first quarter of the year.

Latest data released by the Ministry of Planning and Development showed that, excluding corporations, total PSDP expenditure by about 33 ministries and divisions amounted to a meagre Rs74.65bn in the first four months, or about 11pc of the total allocation of Rs682bn. The corporations — chiefly the power sector and the National Highways Authority — together spent Rs29bn or 9.3pc against their budget allocation of Rs313bn for the whole year.

Ministries, divisions utilise just Rs103.87bn in July-October against Rs1tr allocation

The NHA could utilise only 5.8pc or Rs13.3bn in four months against its annual allocation of Rs225bn. The power sector was able to use Rs16bn or 18pc of its Rs98bn allocation. The Planning Commission had authorised disbursement of Rs78.6bn for NHA and Rs31bn to the power sector.

Under the mechanism announced by the Ministry of Finance for the current fiscal year, the government should release 15pc of budgeted allocation in the first quarter, followed by 20pc in the second quarter, 25pc in the third quarter and the remaining in the last quarter of the fiscal year to ensure that any shortfall in revenue collection is managed through cuts in the development budget to remain with fiscal targets set with the IMF.

Under this mechanism, the Planning Commission claimed that it had authorised Rs303bn for disbursement to the federal ministries in the first four months, which accounted for more than 44pc of the annual target (Rs1tr) and was higher than allowed in the finance ministry’s instructions, but only Rs75bn or 11pc, could actually be spent on the ground.

Only eight ministries were able to cross the Rs1bn spending threshold in 4MFY27, led by the Water Resources Division, which spent Rs18.7bn, or 18pc of its Rs103bn annual allocation. This was followed by Rs6.88bn expenditure in Federal Education and Professional Training against its Rs36bn allocation, accounting for 19pc. Then came Rs6.6bn spending by National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination Division, achieving a healthy rate of 41pc against its allocated share of Rs16bn.

As such, NHSRC exceeded the utilisation target, which was even better when seen in the context of Rs9.6bn authorisation.

Next was Higher Education Commission with a funding utilisation of Rs4.7bn or 10pc of Rs46bn annual allocation. This was followed by the Ministry of Railways with Rs4.65bn utilisation, accounting for around 11pc of its Rs40.65bn allocation. The Ministry of Planning and Development itself used only Rs2.15bn, or less than 10pc, against its allocated share of Rs22.6bn.

After that, the Ministry of Information Technology used only Rs1.45bn or only 7.4pc of its Rs19.6bn allocation.

Combined spending in provinces and special areas (Azad Kashmir and GB) for development amounted to Rs23.8bn, or just 10pc of the annual allocation of Rs233bn and the Planning Commission’s authorisation of Rs59.8bn for the first four months. These special areas are provided funds by the finance division under a separate seasonal pattern.

Likewise, despite the country being at risk of climate disasters, the climate change division spent only Rs259 million in four months or only 10.4pc of its Rs2.5bn allocation. Another critical social-sector ministry — National Food Security — utilised less than 1.5pc (Rs65m) of its allocation of Rs4.2bn.

About six federal ministries could not spend even a single rupee for development in four months.

They included commerce, communication, Kashmir Affairs, Gilgit-Baltistan and states and frontier regions, petroleum, privatisation, religious affairs and interfaith harmony.

Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

headline: Iran urges US to meet terms for Hormuz opening
description: Araghchi says reopening proposal remains on table; Rubio sees no need for major combat operations as economic pressure continues.
author: Agencies
article_text:
• Araghchi says reopening proposal remains on table• Rubio sees no need for major combat operations as economic pressure continues• Qatar PM joins G7 talks after meeting Trump; US president sees ‘positive momentum’• Iran says three oil tankers on fire in Hormuz; October LNG traffic hits post-war high

TEHRAN: Iran on Tuesday urged the United States to accept its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, insisting that diplomacy rather than military action or further sanctions was the only way to end the war, as President Donald Trump saw “positive momentum” towards resolving the conflict.

The diplomatic push gained traction as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no need for major combat operations against Iran, while Qatar’s prime minister joined European and Saudi diplomats for talks on the crisis on the sidelines of a G7 meeting in Paris.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran’s proposal to reopen the strategic waterway within two days of an agreement with Washington remained on the table.

“The conflict with Iran will not be resolved through military means, nor by intensifying sanctions,” Araghchi told the official IRNA news agency.

“The only solution is to adopt a language of respect, engage in diplomacy and address Iran’s demands and conditions — which were outlined in the two-day proposal and remain on the table,” he added.

Iran’s conditions include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing its assets abroad, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

However, Washington insists that nuclear issues must feature in the initial negotiations.

Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei struck a more confrontational tone, urging Washington to “surrender” to Tehran’s demands.

“The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government. But Washington flails like a desperate gambler. FOLD YOUR HAND,” he posted on X.

US sees diplomatic progress

Speaking after a meeting of G7 foreign ministers in Paris, Rubio said Wash­ington’s economic pressure campaign had made further major attacks unnecessary.

“The economic campaign (against Iran) is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations,” he said. “That’s what I told our allies here today.”

Rubio’s remarks followed President Trump’s statement on Monday that the United States was seeing progress towards ending the conflict, which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb 28.

“We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America’s interests are at all times protected,” Trump wrote on social media after meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdu­lrahman Al Thani at the White House.

The US president said further strikes were “quite unlikely”, although he maintained that Washington was “locked and loaded” if necessary.

Meanwhile, Qatar’s prime minister joined discussions with the foreign ministers of Britain, Germany, Italy, France and Saudi Arabia on the sidelines of the G7 meeting in Paris on Tuesday.

The talks, convened by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, focused on the Iran crisis and its security and economic repercussions for the region and the wider international community.

European diplomats have been urging Washington to avoid another military escalation and help restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Three tankers burning

Despite the diplomatic activity, vessels continued to come under attack in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday that three oil tankers were on fire in the waterway, although they did not identify the vessels or provide details of the incidents.

The Emirati state oil company ADNOC said on Tuesday that one of its vessels had “sustained damage following an attack in the UAE’s territorial waters”, while the British maritime agency UKMTO reported a tanker was “struck by an unknown projectile” off the Omani coast.

Meanwhile, the number of loaded liquefied natural gas (LNG) tankers exiting the Strait of Hormuz reached its highest monthly level since the war began, according to vessel-tracking data released on Tuesday.

Data from S&P Global Energy showed that 31 laden LNG tankers passed through the waterway in October, up from 23 in September.

Of the October total, 23 vessels had loaded at Qatar’s Ras Laffan export terminal and eight at Das Island in the United Arab Emirates.

Separately, ship-tracking firm Kpler reported that 42 LNG cargoes were loaded in October, compared with 27 in September.

One vessel, Al Mafyar, transferred LNG to Shandong Redwood and Ejnan, both of which delivered the cargoes to Pakistan.

headline: Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles as strikes hit Sanaa
description: Coalition says it also shot down a drone; Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh airport and oil facility.
author: Agencies
article_text:
• Coalition says it also shot down a drone; Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh airport and oil facility • Officials inspect damaged Aramco building

RIYADH / SANAA: The Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said on Tuesday it had shot down missiles fired by Yemen’s Houthis towards several Saudi cities, amid an escalation in hostilities, while the Houthis reported Saudi air strikes on the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.

The coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile and a cruise missile fired by the group towards Riyadh, as well as a ballistic missile aimed at the kingdom’s southern region and a drone over the oil-rich east.

Saudi civil defence authorities issued alerts in the capital and the southern cities of Abha and Khamis Mushait, later saying the threats had passed.

In the early hours of the morning, AFP journalists heard blasts, while residents received a mobile-phone alert urging them to shelter from an “aerial threat”.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an oil facility in Abqaiq in the east. There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.

The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported that Saudi Arabia had carried out air strikes on Sanaa, hitting a petrol station in the Jadar district north of the capital and a building belonging to the state oil company in southern Sanaa.

Hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been escalating. Riyadh leads a military coalition that has backed Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which was driven from Sanaa by the Houthis more than a decade ago.

The Houthis said on Tuesday they had attacked Saudi Arabia’s vital East-West Pipeline in Riyadh province, while denying a Saudi claim that they had targeted the pipeline in the Madina region. Saudi state media reported on Monday that an attack on the pipeline in Madina province had caused a limited fire but had not affected operations.

Riyadh’s schoolchildren, after two days back in the classroom, returned to online learning on Tuesday “as part of the ongoing precautionary measures”, according to a message to parents on Monday evening.

Aramco office inspected

The latest developments came two days after the Houthis struck a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Aramco in Riyadh’s financial district.

The Houthi attacks have cast a shadow over Saudi Arabia’s efforts to overhaul its oil-reliant economy by attracting foreign investment and promoting tourism and leisure spending.

Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District is one of the most visible manifestations of the drive, with towering glass skyscrapers, high-end retail outlets and green spaces.

Images released by the Saudi Press Agency on Tuesday showed Riyadh officials inspecting the distinctively designed Aramco Tower, with visible damage to several floors.

Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

headline: Opposition moves
description: Expectations of the maulana leading another street confrontation with the government anytime soon are likely to remain wishful thinking.
author: Editorial
article_text:
THE opposition alliance TTAP has hinted at another anti-government drive. Its recent talks with the JUI-F on parliamentary coordination indicate that the party’s chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman is poised to lead the campaign.

All this raises obvious questions: is the opposition seriously planning an anti-government drive? Is it actually convinced that such a movement at this time can remove the government? Will the pragmatic JUI-F chief join such an effort? At least for now, the answer may disappoint the opposition’s supporters.

The PTI is locked in a protracted battle with the government, while much of its top leadership remains behind bars. It has twice attempted to mobilise public support for a mass movement and rally people around its political objectives since the controversial February 2024 elections, but both attempts failed. It is obvious that people, particularly in Punjab and Sindh, are not ready to join any such movement at this time. Even in KP, where the PTI had been in power since 2013, the party has failed to mobilise the public.

The Jamaat-i-Islami’s drive against high petrol prices similarly failed to bring people out onto the streets.

Though the JUI-F has staunch supporters on the streets who are ready to answer their party’s call, its leader has never been one to take needless risks. His azadi march against the PTI government brought thousands of supporters to Islamabad, but failed to dislodge the Imran Khan administration. The sit-in was eventually called off without achieving its objective.

The federal government has imposed emergency measures and governor’s rule in KP, claiming they were necessary for security and administrative reasons. The opposition sees these moves as an assault on provincial autonomy.

Maulana Fazlur Rahman is actively opposing the move. The government’s response to his criticism has fuelled fears that the JUI-F could face the same crackdown as the PTI. Those concerns are not difficult to understand.

The recent actions of the Balochistan government against JUI-F Senator Kamran Murtaza on a questionable citizenship claim reinforce these fears. Yet expectations of the maulana leading another street confrontation with the government anytime soon are likely to remain wishful thinking.

Nevertheless, this consensus of politicians of different persuasions reflects a growing frustration with the government’s high-handed actions.

The lawyers’ emergence in this arena is particularly significant. The All Pakistan Lawyers Action Committee in Quetta has vowed to support Senator Murtaza and resist any attempt to undermine constitutional supremacy. There are also reports of raids on lawyers’ homes.

Although the prospects of a new anti-government movement remain remote, public discontent should not be ignored. Small, isolated protests and expressions of dissent can gradually gather momentum and develop into a much larger movement.

Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

headline: Fazlur Rehman’s son skips NAB summons
description: The bureau usually issues second and third notices before taking punitive action, including arrest, if the accused continues to ignore the summons.
author: Syed Irfan Raza
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: Defying a summons from the Na­­tional Accountability Bu­­reau (NAB), Asad Meh­m­ood, son of Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam (JUI-F) chief Mau­lana Fazlur Rahman, fai­­led to appear before the anti-graft watchdog on Monday in a case concerning alle­ged irregularities in appoi­ntments at Pakistan Post.

NAB, meanwhile, remained tight-lipped about its next course of action. In such cases, the bureau usually issues second and third notices before taking punitive action, including arrest, if the accused continues to ignore the summons.

Mr Mehmood had been directed to appear before the investigation team at 11am on Nov 10 to explain his position on alleged irregularities in 4,252 appointments made at Pakistan Post during his tenure as federal minister in 2022-23.

When contacted, a senior NAB official declined to disclose the bureau’s future course of action, saying that under the new laws, details of investigations could not be shared with the media until the relevant court had decided the case.

According to the notice, the Establishment Division had authorised recruitment against 3,938 posts at Pakistan Post, but 4,252 people were allegedly appointed, exceeding the approved strength. Of these, 2,646 appointments were reportedly made against posts that had already been abolished, in violation of a cabinet committee’s directions.

The bureau is also examining allegations that permanent appointments were made despite a recommendation for contractual recruitment, placing an additional financial burden on Pakistan Post. The alleged political affiliations of some selected candidates are also under scrutiny.

Other allegations include the use of forged documents, recruitment of over-age candidates and violations of the domicile quota.

Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

headline: PM Shehbaz to outline Pakistan’s climate priorities at COP31
description: Premier to meet Erdogan, other world leaders on sidelines of UN climate conference; Musadik Malik says Islamabad seeking global cooperation on glacier research.
author: Syed Irfan Raza
article_text:
• Premier to meet Erdogan, other world leaders on sidelines of UN climate conference • Musadik Malik says Islamabad seeking global cooperation on glacier research • Aleem Khan reaffirms commitment to green freight corridors and low-carbon logistics

ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is set to highlight Pakistan’s climate priorities at the COP31 Antalya Leaders’ Summit in Turkiye today, as Islamabad reaffirmed its commitment to decarbonising global supply chains, while highlighting the threats posed by melting glaciers and the growing risk of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) to vulnerable communities.

On the sidelines of the summit, the prime minister is scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and other world leaders attending COP31 to discuss matters of mutual interest and explore avenues for strengthening bilateral cooperation.

At the conference, the prime minister will highlight Pakistan’s climate priorities and stress the urgent need for enhanced global climate action and stronger international cooperation to mitigate the adverse impacts of climate change in line with established principles.

He will also address a high-level dialogue on clean energy transition and electrification titled “35 by 35: Powering the Future”.

Melting glaciers

Earlier, speaking at the UN Climate Cha­nge Pavilion at COP31, Federal Minis­ter for Climate Change Musadik Malik called for international scientific cooperation to study glaciers and mountain ecosystems, saying the first impacts of climate change were often felt in mountainous regions.

He said more than 13,500 glaciers had been identified in Pakistan, while the growing threat of glacial lake outburst floods required coordinated scientific research and international cooperation.

“Pakistan contributes less than one per cent to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet it remains among the countries most severely affected by climate change,” he said.

He warned that melting glaciers were putting thousands of people, their homes and sources of livelihood at risk, adding that climate change was not merely an environmental challenge but a question of human survival.

The minister called for an equitable distribution of climate finance, saying developing countries facing severe climate impacts needed timely financial assistance. He observed that climate financing remained concentrated among major emitting countries, despite the vulnerability of nations contributing little to global emissions.

He said scientific research in mountainous regions could also improve understanding of climate risks in plains and polar regions, stressing the need to move beyond international declarations towards practical cooperation.

Highlighting Pakistan’s proposed initiatives to promote research and innovation, Mr Malik outlined plans for a Green Virtual University to connect Pakistani students, researchers and faculty members with leading international universities and scientists.

Green freight corridors

Meanwhile, Federal Minister for Communications Aleem Khan reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to decarbonising global supply chains and building climate-resilient logistics infrastructure while addressing a high-level ministerial roundtable on the Global Green Freight Corridors Initiative during COP31 in Antalya.

Mr Khan said international freight transport served as the lifeblood of global commerce but remained one of the fastest-growing sources of transport-related greenhouse gas emissions.

Emphasising that economic growth and environmental protection were mutually reinforcing goals, he said the launch of the Global Green Freight Corridors Initiative demonstrated that sustainable logistics was essential for the future.

Endorsing the initiative and its four key pillars — clean technology, digital connectivity, smart route planning and climate finance — the minister expressed Pakistan’s full support for collaboration with international partners on pilot green corridors. He stressed that as the international community focused on the objectives of COP31, efforts should shift towards translating climate commitments into tangible cross-border outcomes.

With additional input from APP

Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

“Pakistan contributes less than one per cent to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet it remains among the countries most severely affected by climate change,” he said.

He warned that melting glaciers were putting thousands of people, their homes and sources of livelihood at risk, adding that climate change was not merely an environmental challenge but a question of human survival.

The minister called for an equitable distribution of climate finance, saying developing countries facing severe climate impacts needed timely financial assistance. He observed that climate financing remained concentrated among major emitting countries, despite the vulnerability of nations contributing little to global emissions.

He said scientific research in mountainous regions could also improve understanding of climate risks in plains and polar regions, stressing the need to move beyond international declarations towards practical cooperation.

Highlighting Pakistan’s proposed initiatives to promote research and innovation, Mr Malik outlined plans for a Green Virtual University to connect Pakistani students, researchers and faculty members with leading international universities and scientists.

Green freight corridors

Meanwhile, Federal Minister for Communications Aleem Khan reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to decarbonising global supply chains and building climate-resilient logistics infrastructure while addressing a high-level ministerial roundtable on the Global Green Freight Corridors Initiative during COP31 in Antalya.

Mr Khan said international freight transport served as the lifeblood of global commerce but remained one of the fastest-growing sources of transport-related greenhouse gas emissions.

Emphasising that economic growth and environmental protection were mutually reinforcing goals, he said the launch of the Global Green Freight Corridors Initiative demonstrated that sustainable logistics was essential for the future.

Endorsing the initiative and its four key pillars — clean technology, digital connectivity, smart route planning and climate finance — the minister expressed Pakistan’s full support for collaboration with international partners on pilot green corridors. He stressed that as the international community focused on the objectives of COP31, efforts should shift towards translating climate commitments into tangible cross-border outcomes.

headline: What money bought
description: A recent book details how money and corruption were leveraged to redesign the Middle East.
author: Zahid Hussain
article_text:
SLEAZE, bribery, and secret alliances allegedly marked Trump’s Middle East policy in his first term, and set him on the road to an illegal and unwinnable war against Iran in his second. The central characters in that sordid set of machinations were his own son-in-law and senior adviser Jared Kushner, a few Gulf rulers, and Israel’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu — all working towards a plan to redraw the political map of West Asia. Iran was the adversary to be contained, and it was on this that they converged: a plan to “blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal”.

Billions of dollars were allegedly paid to Kushner in what may be the biggest scandal in recent history — one that best defines the link between money and Trump’s conduct of his Middle East policy, and which has pushed the entire region into an intractable conflict with global consequences.

A recently published book, Princes and Thieves by investigative journalist Matthew Cole, provides startling details on how billions of dollars were allegedly transferred into accounts — managed by Kushner — by Gulf sheikhdoms, to implement a plan to break Obama’s nuclear deal with Iran and change the “political map of the Middle East”. The author supports his view of the transactions with details drawn from accounts hacked by a Western intelligence agency, though Kushner has called the allegations fabricated.

According to the author, the transfers began in 2017 and were well underway by the spring of 2018, during Trump’s first term — when Kushner served as the president’s special envoy on the Middle East. While he had very close relations with Israel, he also cultivated strong business and diplomatic connections with willing Gulf sheikhdoms to allegedly pay for influence with the Trump administration.

>A recent book details how money and corruption were leveraged to redesign the Middle East.

According to the author, “Kushner, UAE ruler Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ), and Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) of Saudi Arabia, converged at an auspicious moment. MBS wanted to be crown prince. MBZ wanted to blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, and Kushner wanted both to help him force the Palestinians into a deal that Israel would accept”. The convergence against Obama’s nuclear deal with Iran — formally the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) — brought Saudi Arabia and the UAE together on the issue.

Agreed on July 14, 2015, between Iran and the P5+1, and endorsed by Security Council Resolution 2231, the deal came into effect in January 2016. Under it, Iran capped its enrichment at 3.67 per cent, cut its centrifuge numbers and opened its nuclear facilities to IAEA inspection. In return, nuclear-related sanctions on Iran were lifted on oil exports, banking, and SWIFT access, with frozen assets to be released in stages.

But Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE had strong reservations. Each opposed the JCPOA for different reasons and with different intensity; the common ground was that the agreement was too narrow and too temporary, its restrictions written to expire under sunset clauses. Israel openly campaigned against it, and the two Gulf states lobbied against it too.

For deal sceptics, Trump’s election in 2016 was good news. In May 2018, the president withdrew from the JCPOA and reimposed sanctions in phases under a “maximum pressure” campaign. The move brought the Gulf nations closer to the Trump administration. The billions alleged to have flowed into Kushner’s accounts appeared to have delivered. The book maintains that early in Trump’s first term, “MBZ and MBS offered to pay for a slush fund dedicated to helping the new administration with foreign policy goals”. Both Arab rulers saw this as part of an effort to help Trump win a second presidency.

In the same period, Kushner conceived the so-called Abraham Accords aimed at normalisation between Israel and the Arab states. He owned the file. No State Department desk, no regional bureau, no ambassador in the chain: a son-in-law with a security clearance and a direct line to the president negotiated directly with the Gulf rulers, according to the book. One goal was to sideline the question of a separate Palestinian state. The UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan signed.

The book also reveals that during that period Kushner helped negotiate a secret warming of diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE — the arrangement that later became public as the Abraham Accords. Cole writes that “Kushner helped negotiate an agreement by Israel to help defend the UAE against a major Iranian military attack. The UAE needed to cover the cost of that emergency defence, and its government secretly made another transfer to Israel’s Central Bank. This was something like a rainy-day defence fund. Combined, the three accounts represented a secret foreign policy negotiated by Kushner with the leaders of Israel, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia.

“Although Kushner’s position as senior adviser to the president was unpaid, he was an official government employee. Not only did his position require financial disclosure for ethics regulations, but each year he worked in the White House he had to file both a public and a confidential financial form, the Executive Branch Personnel Public Financial Disclosure Report, known as a 278e disclosure. Because he had access to classified government secrets, Kushner was required to disclose any bank account to which he had signatory — or beneficiary — access.” But apparently, the president’s son-in-law did not comply.

The writer quotes a source that Kushner “promised MBZ he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalisation with Israel so that business could take off”. For the Gulf Arab governments, money was not a problem. “The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent,” the source told the author.

The book exposes the sordid linkage between power and corruption that marked Trump’s presidency. It also lays bare the unholy alliance between Israel and the Gulf governments, formed to change the political map of the Middle East. In the end, this design has left the region more destabilised than before.

The writer is an author and journalist.

headline: Twenty hurt in two accidents
description: Four people were injured when a Karachi-bound speeding car overturned after going out of control of the driver on Makran coastal highway.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Correspondent
article_text:
QUETTA: Twenty people were injured in two separate road accidents on the coastal highway in Makran and Qila Saifullah areas on Tuesday.

According to police, four people were injured when a Karachi-bound speeding car overturned after going out of control of the driver on Makran coastal highway.

The injured were immediately taken to Uthal district headquarters hospital. In another road accident, 16 people were injured when two passenger coaches collided at the Gawal Ismail Zai area of Qila Saifullah.

headline: Unclaimed accounts
description: THE State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) recently issued a public notice with respect to un- claimed deposits in banks. The...
author: From the Newspaper
article_text:
THE State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) recently issued a public notice with respect to un-

claimed deposits in banks. The magnitude and the volume of unclaimed deposits would not have grown humongous had the regulators and the banks kept a close liaison with their customers and followed the laid down standard operating procedures (SOPs).

As per banking practices, customers furnish the details of the next of kin while opening their bank account. Is there an exercise undertaken to contact the next of kin to verify the whereabouts of the customers before unilaterally closing the account and transferring money to SBP as unclaimed funds? My sister had lodged an application for a refund of unclaimed deposit with a bank branch in Islamabad some four years ago. She is still waiting for a response.

An exercise, though indeed painstaking, needs to be undertaken by the SBP in collaboration with the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) to confirm the existence or otherwise of all the account holders whose deposits happen to be lying with the central bank.

The assignment could be outsourced, if needed. In case the account holder has died, the unclaimed deposit in the said account should be refunded to the legal heirs through a public announcement. In case no trace is found, the amount should be donated to some charity organisation as is the practice in some other countries.

KhaledIslamabad

headline: US fails to show for UN rights review, yet again
description: The country becomes only second nation to boycott UN review after Israel in 2013.
author: AFP
article_text:
GENEVA: The United States boycotted on Tuesday a United Nations review of its human rights record for a second time, in an unprecedented snub of a process that all countries traditionally submit to. US seats were left empty at the world body’s European headquarters in Geneva for the so-called Universal Periodic Review (UPR), which all 193 UN member states undergo every four to five years.

As the review was set to begin, UN Human Rights Council president Sidharto Reza Suryodipuro, of Indonesia, looked at the empty seats behind the US nameplate and said that “the delegation of the United States is not present in the room”.

The US absence was not a surprise. President Donald Trump’s administration decided shortly after his return to power in January 2025 to halt cooperation with the rights council, and had already boycotted the UPR process last November.

In response, the council at the time had postponed the US review for a year, in the hope that Washington would return. The US State Department said this week that the administration considers the council an “irredeemable body” that “makes a mockery of human rights”, suggesting that it would not participate in any of its mechanisms, including the UPR.

‘Accountability is important’

Despite the continued boycott, rights advocates, civil society organisations and US elected officials have gathered in Geneva this week to keep a spotlight on alleged US rights abuses. Among them was Noor Abdalla, the wife of Mahmoud Khalil, the prominent pro-Palestinian protest leader and green card holder whom the Trump administration sought to deport last year. “Accountability is important,” she told reporters.

“When the most powerful government in the world is not held acc­o­­untable, they think that they can do whatever they want to do… We saw that with my husband’s case.” Washington’s complete non-compliance with the process is unprecedented. Before the United States, only Israel had previously boycotted its UPR, in early 2013, although it underwent a delayed review later that year. Some countries have sought postponements since the UPR process began in 2008, while Nicaragua partially boycotted the process, but only after its latest review had already taken place.

‘Hypocrisy’

Several diplomats spoke up on Tuesday about the value of the UPR, with the European Union representative saying Brussels “regrets any situation in which full engagement… does not occur, including the decision by the United States again not to participate”. Cuban ambassador Rodolfo Benitez Verson voiced outrage at Washington’s absence.

“The United States is the only country in the history of the Human Rights Council which has refused to take part in the UPR cycle without even presenting its national report,” he told the council, slamming US “double standards and hypocrisy”.

headline: World powers have to adjust their ways
description: THE world is not changing hands; it is actually changing shape. The age in which one superpower could dominate the...
author: From the Newspaper
article_text:
THE world is not changing hands; it is actually changing shape. The age in which one superpower could dominate the global conversation is now giving way to an era where influence is scattered, contested and increasingly difficult to sustain. For decades, the United States stood at the centre of the international system. However, things are changing, steadily altering the global balance.

The US remains a military, financial and technological giant. The dollar continues to occupy a central position in international finance, while American universities, technology companies and security partnerships provide Washington with enormous global influence. What is changing is not America’s importance, but its ability to shape international outcomes without facing serious resistance.

China is at the heart of this transforma- tion. Its economic scale, manufacturing capacity and expanding diplomatic presence have made it impossible to discuss global politics without China. Yet, describing

the future as simply a transition from an American to a Chinese world would be misleading. China may seek greater influence, but the international system is too complex for one rising power to inherit the entire US supremacy.

India represents another important centre of gravity owing to its enormous population, expanding economy, techno-

logical capacity and strategic importance which together give it enough room to pursue an independent foreign policy. Rather than permanently aligning itself with one camp, New Delhi has demons-trated the value of maintaining relation-ships with competing powers. This reflects a broader trend among countries across the Global South.

For most of the developing states, foreign policy is no longer about choosing between Washington and Beijing. It is now about extracting maximum benefit from both. They want Chinese investment, Western markets, Russian energy, Gulf capital and strategic cooperation with a multitude of partners. Such flexibility is becoming a diplomatic asset.

The growing importance of BRICS and other alternative platforms also reflects dissatisfaction with a global system in which decision-making has often been concentrated among a limited group of powerful states. However, these emerging groupings are not unified blocs. Their members have competing interests and a variety of political priorities. Their importance lies less in replacing the West than in making the global system a lot more pluralistic.

At the same time, power itself is now becoming fragmented. Military strength remains crucial, but control over semi-conductors, artificial intelligence (AI), energy, critical minerals, food supplies, data and financial networks can be equally consequential. A country may be powerful in one domain while depending heavily on another state in a different one.

This fragmentation carries risks. More centres of power can give smaller states greater choices, but they can also make global politics unpredictable. Trade disputes can become security disputes; techno-logical competition can become diplomatic confrontation; and economic dependence can become a strategic vulnerability. The world, therefore, is moving towards a much more contested international order. Will competing powers learn to coexist in a world where none is powerful enough to dictate the rules alone? The answer to this question will define the coming decades.

headline: Father and son among seven killed by Israeli fire in Gaza Strip
description: Unicef says Tel Aviv blocks Gaza basin repairs, warns of flood risk.
author: Agencies
article_text:
RAMALLAH/GENEVA: Israeli forces killed at least seven Pales­tinians, including a father and his 13-year-old son, in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, local health officials said.

Medics said Fadi Rajab and his son Abubakr were killed in an airstrike that hit the roof of a displacement shelter in the Zeitoun neighbourhood in Gaza City. A third Palestinian was killed in an Israeli airstrike near a school in Gaza City’s Daraj neighbourhood, health officials added.

In Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, Israeli gunfire killed a man, medics said. Later on Tuesday, an Israeli airstrike hit a metal foundry in the Sabra neighbourhood of Gaza City, killing three people, medics said, taking the day’s death toll to at least seven.

Israeli forces shot dead a 14-year-old in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials said, with Israel saying it was responding to stone-throwing.

Moutaz Eyad Daghlas was killed in Burqa, northwest of Nablus, late on Monday, the Palestinian health ministry said.

Unicef says Tel Aviv blocks Gaza basin repairs, warns of flood risk

The Palestine Red Crescent Society said its teams treated two people with gunshot wounds and took them to hospital, but that Israeli forces blocked access to a third wounded person and detained three volunteer paramedics.

Israeli forces have routinely opened live fire on Palestinians including minors who throw stones in the West Bank, which Israel has controlled since 1967.

The Israeli human rights group B’Tselem said Israeli forces killed at least 241 children or teenagers in the territory between the Oct 7, 2023 raid by Hamas and late June this year.

Violence has increased in recent weeks, especially in the run-up to Israel’s Oct 27 election, before which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had sought to appeal to hardline settlers in the West Bank.

On Oct 23, Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint near Hebron before being killed by Israeli forces, who later responded with a major operation in the flashpoint city.

Flood risk in Gaza

The UN children’s agency said Israel had rejected the importation of equipment needed to repair a water basin in Gaza, and warned that the facility could overflow and endanger nearby residents through flooding and disease.

Local authorities say Israel destroyed water infrastructure and vehicles used to pump water during its war against Hamas, which had displaced most of the territory’s more than two million residents and left much of Gaza in ruins. Most of the population now lives in tent camps.

One damaged facility is the Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin in Gaza City, which is now contaminated with sewage and at risk of overflowing after heavy rainfall, according to Unicef’s James Elder.

He told reporters the agency had been working with Israeli authorities and US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace for a year on a $3 million plan to repair it, but that COGAT, the Israeli military agency overseeing humanitarian affairs in Gaza, had rejected the project in the past few days.

“Toxic sewage could flow into the streets and tents of Gaza City, forcing children and families from their makeshift homes once more, and grossly increasing the threat of disease. So we’re a bit baffled,” he told a press briefing in Geneva. “Let’s do the rehabilitation before this becomes another entirely preventable killer of girls and boys in Gaza,” he said.

This week, heavy rain has already flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians crammed into encampments across the Gaza Strip. Four people, including three small children, were killed when a sand embankment collapsed on their tents in an incident that highlighted the risks ahead of the rainy winter season.

A US-brokered ceasefire last year called for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel to withdraw its troops.

World Health Organisation spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said at the same briefing there were significant communicable disease risks in Gaza due to flooding, poor sanitation and insufficient health and water services. Nearly 1 million displaced people across Gaza now faced medium or high flood risk, he said.

RAMALLAH/GENEVA: Israeli forces killed at least seven Pales­tinians, including a father and his 13-year-old son, in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, local health officials said.

Medics said Fadi Rajab and his son Abubakr were killed in an airstrike that hit the roof of a displacement shelter in the Zeitoun neighbourhood in Gaza City. A third Palestinian was killed in an Israeli airstrike near a school in Gaza City’s Daraj neighbourhood, health officials added.

In Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, Israeli gunfire killed a man, medics said. Later on Tuesday, an Israeli airstrike hit a metal foundry in the Sabra neighbourhood of Gaza City, killing three people, medics said, taking the day’s death toll to at least seven.

Israeli forces shot dead a 14-year-old in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials said, with Israel saying it was responding to stone-throwing.

Moutaz Eyad Daghlas was killed in Burqa, northwest of Nablus, late on Monday, the Palestinian health ministry said.

Unicef says Tel Aviv blocks Gaza basin repairs, warns of flood risk

The Palestine Red Crescent Society said its teams treated two people with gunshot wounds and took them to hospital, but that Israeli forces blocked access to a third wounded person and detained three volunteer paramedics.

Israeli forces have routinely opened live fire on Palestinians including minors who throw stones in the West Bank, which Israel has controlled since 1967.

The Israeli human rights group B’Tselem said Israeli forces killed at least 241 children or teenagers in the territory between the Oct 7, 2023 raid by Hamas and late June this year.

Violence has increased in recent weeks, especially in the run-up to Israel’s Oct 27 election, before which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had sought to appeal to hardline settlers in the West Bank.

On Oct 23, Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint near Hebron before being killed by Israeli forces, who later responded with a major operation in the flashpoint city.

Flood risk in Gaza

The UN children’s agency said Israel had rejected the importation of equipment needed to repair a water basin in Gaza, and warned that the facility could overflow and endanger nearby residents through flooding and disease.

Local authorities say Israel destroyed water infrastructure and vehicles used to pump water during its war against Hamas, which had displaced most of the territory’s more than two million residents and left much of Gaza in ruins. Most of the population now lives in tent camps.

One damaged facility is the Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin in Gaza City, which is now contaminated with sewage and at risk of overflowing after heavy rainfall, according to Unicef’s James Elder.

He told reporters the agency had been working with Israeli authorities and US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace for a year on a $3 million plan to repair it, but that COGAT, the Israeli military agency overseeing humanitarian affairs in Gaza, had rejected the project in the past few days.

“Toxic sewage could flow into the streets and tents of Gaza City, forcing children and families from their makeshift homes once more, and grossly increasing the threat of disease. So we’re a bit baffled,” he told a press briefing in Geneva. “Let’s do the rehabilitation before this becomes another entirely preventable killer of girls and boys in Gaza,” he said.

This week, heavy rain has already flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians crammed into encampments across the Gaza Strip. Four people, including three small children, were killed when a sand embankment collapsed on their tents in an incident that highlighted the risks ahead of the rainy winter season.

A US-brokered ceasefire last year called for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel to withdraw its troops.

World Health Organisation spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said at the same briefing there were significant communicable disease risks in Gaza due to flooding, poor sanitation and insufficient health and water services. Nearly 1 million displaced people across Gaza now faced medium or high flood risk, he said.
